In the short run, a perfectly competitive firm takes the market price as given. The firm’s individual demand curve is perfectly elastic at that market price, so its marginal revenue (MR) equals the market price P.
• Profit maximization condition: The firm produces the quantity of output where marginal cost (MC) equals marginal revenue (MR), which is the same as price in perfect competition: MC = MR = P, provided that P ≥ AVC at that quantity.
• Shutdown decision:
  – If P ≥ AVC at the point where MC = MR, the firm continues producing because it can cover its variable costs and at least some of its fixed costs.
  – If P < AVC at all output levels, the firm minimizes its loss by shutting down and producing zero output in the short run.
• Profit or loss:
  – If P > ATC at Q*, the firm earns economic profit. Profit per unit is P − ATC; total profit is (P − ATC) × Q*.
  – If P = ATC at Q*, the firm earns zero economic profit (normal profit).
  – If AVC ≤ P < ATC at Q*, the firm operates at a loss in the short run but stays open because it still covers variable costs and part of fixed costs.
Graphically, the MC curve above the minimum point of AVC is the firm’s short‑run supply curve. The intersection of P = MR with the MC curve gives the profit‑maximizing quantity Q*. ATC and AVC evaluated at Q* determine whether the firm is making profits, breaking even, or incurring losses.

Demand‑pull inflation arises when aggregate demand in an economy grows faster than aggregate supply, pushing the overall price level upward. Common causes include expansionary fiscal policy (higher government spending or tax cuts), expansionary monetary policy (low interest rates, rapid money growth), or surges in private consumption and investment.
• Example: A booming economy with rising incomes and optimistic expectations leads to strong consumer spending and business investment. With the economy near full employment, this extra demand pushes prices up.
• Policy responses:
  – Contractionary monetary policy: central bank raises interest rates, reduces money supply growth to dampen spending.
  – Contractionary fiscal policy: government reduces spending or increases taxes to lower aggregate demand.

Cost‑push inflation occurs when production costs rise, causing firms to reduce supply or raise prices even if demand is unchanged. Typical causes include rising wages not matched by productivity gains, increases in the prices of key inputs (e.g., oil), or supply shocks such as natural disasters.
• Example: A sharp increase in global oil prices raises transportation and production costs for many firms; they pass these higher costs on to consumers, causing a general rise in prices, even if demand is weak.
• Policy responses:
  – Supply‑side policies: improve productivity (investment in infrastructure, education, deregulation where appropriate) to lower unit costs over time.
  – Targeted support: temporary subsidies or tax relief for heavily affected sectors, or targeted income support for households facing higher living costs.
  – Monetary policy: central bank faces a trade‑off. Tightening policy can contain inflation expectations but may worsen unemployment; accommodating cost shocks risks entrenching higher inflation. Many central banks partly tighten while communicating a medium‑term commitment to their inflation target.
